(Se'if katan 2) We train, etc. See there in Tosafos. This is in Tosafos Yeshanim, and so too in Terumas HaDeshen, siman 94. They asked about what we learned in Yoma 82, that we train minors by hours: but a minor who eats neveilos, the court is not commanded to separate him. If so, can we train them, when separation itself should be required? Rabbeinu Yitzchak answered that training minors applies only to the father, but not to another person, and therefore they are not commanded to separate him. They asked from the case at the beginning of Sukkah, that Queen Helen sat with her seven sons in a sukkah, which shows that even where there is no father, training applies. They answered: perhaps they had a father who trained them for this; and even if they had no father, their mother trained them only as a general mitzvah matter. End quote of Tosafos. So too in the Terumas HaDeshen mentioned above. Tosafos wrote similarly in Nazir 28b, and on page 29a the Gemara concludes explicitly according to Reish Lakish that a mother is not obligated to train her son. Although Rabbi Yochanan there disagrees with Reish Lakish, and according to Rabbi Yochanan it is not necessary to say that a woman is not obligated to train her son, nevertheless it is better to minimize the dispute and say that Rabbi Yochanan too agrees with Reish Lakish on this point. See above in the Magen Avraham, siman 343.
Nevertheless, it seems to me that she should not give, etc. Meaning, the mother, although she is not obligated in training.
And it is not comparable to sukkah, where she is permitted, etc. For if you would not say so, what did Tosafos ask from Queen Helen sitting with her seven sons in a sukkah, as above? It would have been forbidden for her to give them food outside the sukkah.
And she is not obligated to bring him in, etc., because the mother is not obligated in training.
Furthermore, there it is a positive commandment. Meaning, eating in the sukkah is a positive commandment.
A negative prohibition is more severe than a positive commandment, as stated in the first chapter of Yevamos in the sugya of 'aleha,' and as is also proven in the second chapter of Yevamos. End quote of Terumas HaDeshen, siman 94. Therefore, since eating in a sukkah is only a positive commandment, even giving them food is permitted. However, the Magen Avraham at the beginning of siman 269 rejected this, according to what we rule that even a rabbinic prohibition may not be fed directly to a minor, all the more so a Torah positive commandment. Therefore one must say that what he wrote here, 'furthermore, there it is a positive commandment,' leaves his first answer primary: sukkah is different, because in the eating itself there is no prohibition. In truth, directly feeding a minor outside the sukkah is forbidden even for a woman, and so he wrote explicitly below in siman 640. Rather, after he previously distinguished that on Yom Kippur the eating itself is prohibited, he now writes another reasoning: even if Yom Kippur were exactly comparable to sukkah in this respect, there is more room for leniency with sukkah, because it is a positive commandment, than with Yom Kippur. However, the Terumas HaDeshen at the end of the responsum challenged the Tosafos mentioned above and proved from Eruvin that the mother too is obligated to train her son, and he concluded that one should not be lenient; see there.
That which is not, etc. In his twelfth year. Meaning, when he is eleven complete years old, as the Rema wrote, one should be lenient only with a thin youth.
Because everyone studies, etc. We rely on Rashi's view in Kesubos 50a according to the Bach's explanation of Rashi's words; see there. But when he is twelve complete years old and enters his thirteenth year, Rashi, and also the Bach, agree that he must complete the fast rabbinically, except for a thin youth, where we rely on the 'some say' opinion brought by the Rema. In Eliyah Rabbah he wrote in the name of the Bach on what the Rema wrote, 'and one may rely on them regarding a youth who is thin': our custom is so with all children, since they all study, and also nowadays they are ordinarily considered sick. In truth, the Bach was lenient only when he is eleven, as above. It is possible that in Eliyah Rabbah he wrote this from his own reasoning based on the Bach's reasoning. And also because ordinarily they are considered sick, meaning nowadays, when weakness has descended to the world. The Bach concluded: since we are not expert when it is danger to life, in a doubt involving life we rule leniently.

5) [Se'if 2] One who wishes to be stringent, etc. Maharshal writes in Yam Shel Shlomo, Bava Kamma, chapter 7, siman 41, that one who publicly acts stringently regarding a permitted matter when there is concern for ostentation is placed under a ban. If he is known to act for the sake of Heaven, he is not banned. If he acts stringently before his rav while his rav is lenient, he is banned even if he acts for the sake of Heaven. Even where the permission is not entirely obvious, he should not be stringent against his rav's ruling unless he has proof refuting it. Magen Avraham, paragraph 2; Soles Belulah, paragraph 2; Eliyah Rabbah, paragraph 4; Chesed LaAlafim, paragraph 2. See Pri Megadim, Eshel Avraham, and Machatzis HaShekel, paragraph 2. Birkei Yosef, paragraph 1, cites Rabbi Menachem of Beis Meir, brought in Shitah Mekubetzes, Bava Kamma 81b: when a matter's permission is obvious, it is improper to be stringent in the presence of one greater in wisdom while that scholar follows the lenient ruling. If he does so, the scholar may place him under a ban. If the stringent person is recognized for piety, however, he may act stringently. See Responsa Maharadakh, end of responsum 26, and Ginnas Veradim, Yoreh Deah, rule 3, end of siman 6.
6) There: One who wishes to be stringent by standing when seated and reciting it standing is called a transgressor. Tur concludes in the name of Rav Amram that one should rebuke him, because the mitzvah is recited while seated. Beis Yosef explains this to mean that it may be recited even while seated. Prishah, paragraph 6, however, writes that it specifically should be recited while seated. Rema in Darkei Moshe, paragraph 1, also appears to hold this. He comments upon Beis Yosef that Hagahos Maimoniyos, chapter 2, implies that sitting is better than standing, apparently disagreeing with Maran and requiring sitting. Pri Chadash, paragraph 2, similarly writes that Tur's statement in the name of Rav Amram means that the principal mitzvah is seated, so that one's mind will be more settled, like the conclusion at the end of the chapter Sheloshah She'achlu that in all those cases the halachah is to sit and recite the blessing. Maamar Mordechai, paragraph 2, cites him and approves. This is also implied by Bereishis Rabbah, chapter 48, on "He was sitting at the entrance of the tent": Rabbi Berechyah in the name of Rabbi Levi says the word is written "sit." Avraham wished to stand, but the Holy One, blessed be He, told him, "Sit." So too your descendants will sit: when Israel enters synagogues and study halls and recites Krias Shema, they sit in My honor, while I stand over them, as it is stated, "God stands in the congregation of the Almighty." The same appears in Bamidbar Rabbah, Parashas Naso, chapter 11, and Midrash Chazis on "My Beloved resembles a gazelle." Yafeh LaLev, paragraph 2. Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 2 concerning the repetition of the Amidah, folio 38d, and Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar Krias Shema, end of chapter 29, likewise imply that since Krias Shema corresponds to the world of Beriah it must be recited while seated. Although Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 6 concerning Krias Shema, folio 22c, writes that we are not obligated to recite it, etc., implying that standing would not matter, according to the mystical teaching sitting remains preferable, as implied by the cited discourse 2 and Pri Etz Chaim. See Ateres Zekenim, paragraph 2, and Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Va'eira, paragraph 16.
7) There: And recite it standing, etc. Sefer HaKanah, cited in the new Tzafnas Pane'ach, says that Krias Shema must be recited standing in Eretz Yisrael and seated outside Eretz Yisrael. This distinction appears not to be accepted by the poskim or kabbalists. Whether in Eretz Yisrael or outside it, all are equal: "the righteous sit." Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi, siman 14, paragraph 32. The same follows from Shaar HaKavanos and Pri Etz Chaim cited in the preceding paragraph: Krias Shema corresponds to the world of Beriah and must therefore be recited seated, with no distinction between Eretz Yisrael and elsewhere. Consider this carefully.
8) There: He is called a transgressor. This implies that he nevertheless fulfilled his obligation. Even according to Rav Yosef, who says that one who acted like Beis Shammai accomplished nothing, this means that he did not fulfill the mitzvah properly. The Gemara compares it to one whose head and most of his body were in a sukkah while his table was inside the house; after the fact he fulfilled the obligation, as Ran writes at the end of Arvei Pesachim regarding the Mishnah's statement that one who did not mention these three matters on Pesach did not fulfill his obligation. Ramban writes similarly in Milchamos at the beginning of Berachos, as does Tur at the end of siman 66. Erekh HaShulchan, paragraph 1. See Mateh Yehudah, paragraph 1, for his discussion. Pischei HaDvir, paragraph 2, agrees with Erekh HaShulchan, and Yafeh LaLev, paragraph 2, appears to agree as well.
9) There: He is called a transgressor. If he stands in order to dispel sleep, it is permitted. Chesed LaAlafim, paragraph 2; Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Va'eira, paragraph 15.

cases.en_html: 6) There: One who wishes to be stringent by standing when seated and reciting it standing is called a transgressor. Tur concludes in the name of Rav Amram that one should rebuke him, because the mitzvah is recited while seated. Beis Yosef explains this to mean that it may be recited even while seated. Prishah, paragraph 6, however, writes that it specifically should be recited while seated. Rema in Darkei Moshe, paragraph 1, also appears to hold this. He comments upon Beis Yosef that Hagahos Maimoniyos, chapter 2, implies that sitting is better than standing, apparently disagreeing with Maran and requiring sitting. Pri Chadash, paragraph 2, similarly writes that Tur's statement in the name of Rav Amram means that the principal mitzvah is seated, so that one's mind will be more settled, like the conclusion at the end of the chapter Sheloshah She'achlu that in all those cases the halachah is to sit and recite the blessing. Maamar Mordechai, paragraph 2, cites him and approves. This is also implied by Bereishis Rabbah, chapter 48, on "He was sitting at the entrance of the tent": Rabbi Berechyah in the name of Rabbi Levi says the word is written "sit." Avraham wished to stand, but the Holy One, blessed be He, told him, "Sit." So too your descendants will sit: when Israel enters synagogues and study halls and recites Krias Shema, they sit in My honor, while I stand over them, as it is stated, "God stands in the congregation of the Almighty." The same appears in Bamidbar Rabbah, Parashas Naso, chapter 11, and Midrash Chazis on "My Beloved resembles a gazelle." Yafeh LaLev, paragraph 2. Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 2 concerning the repetition of the Amidah, folio 38d, and Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar Krias Shema, end of chapter 29, likewise imply that since Krias Shema corresponds to the world of Beriah it must be recited while seated. Although Shaar HaKavanos, discourse 6 concerning Krias Shema, folio 22c, writes that we are not obligated to recite it, etc., implying that standing would not matter, according to the mystical teaching sitting remains preferable, as implied by the cited discourse 2 and Pri Etz Chaim. See Ateres Zekenim, paragraph 2, and Ben Ish Chai, Parashas Va'eira, paragraph 16.

cases.he_html: ז) שם ולקרותה מעומד וכו'. מ"ש בספר הקנה והביאו בס' צפנת פענח חדש דבא"י צ"ל הק"ש מעומד ובחו"ל מיושב כיעו"ש נראה דאינו מוסכם דבר זה מהפוסקים ומבעלי הקבלה ובין בארץ ובין בחו"ל כולן שוין צדיקים יושבים. כף החיים להרח"פ ז"ל סי' י"ד אות ל"ב. וכ"מ ממ"ש באות הקודם בשם שער הכוונות ופע"ח דק"ש היא בבחי' עולם הבריאה ולכך צ"ל מיושב וזה אין חילוק לארץ ולחו"ל ודו"ק:
cases.en_html: 7) There: And recite it standing, etc. Sefer HaKanah, cited in the new Tzafnas Pane'ach, says that Krias Shema must be recited standing in Eretz Yisrael and seated outside Eretz Yisrael. This distinction appears not to be accepted by the poskim or kabbalists. Whether in Eretz Yisrael or outside it, all are equal: "the righteous sit." Kaf HaChaim by Rabbi Chaim Palagi, siman 14, paragraph 32. The same follows from Shaar HaKavanos and Pri Etz Chaim cited in the preceding paragraph: Krias Shema corresponds to the world of Beriah and must therefore be recited seated, with no distinction between Eretz Yisrael and elsewhere. Consider this carefully.
